title: Component vs end-to-end evaluation
summary: Component evals score one stage with the other stages held fixed, so a fault points at a layer. End-to-end evals score the whole system on the user's task, so they say whether users are affected. Use many cheap component checks and fewer expensive end-to-end ones.
useIf: A pipeline has several stages (retrieve, rerank, generate, call tools) and you need to know which one broke.
avoidIf: The system is a single model call with no retrieval or tools, where one end-to-end score is the component.

explain.md: **End-to-end** evaluation treats the system as a black box: a question goes in, an answer comes out, and you grade the answer against the user's task. It is what users feel, but a low score does not say where the fault is. **Component** evaluation fixes the inputs to one stage and scores only that stage: retrieval with rank metrics, generation given a fixed context, tool selection given a fixed plan, a router or a guardrail as a classifier.

Think of a test pyramid. Hamel Husain describes three levels: fast assertions run on every code change, model and human evaluation on a set cadence, and A/B tests after significant product changes, with cost rising at each level [[tr6]]. Foundry's suggested combinations follow the same idea: RAG is Retrieval, Groundedness, Relevance and Content Safety; agents are Output Quality, Tool Use Quality, Rubric and Content Safety [[r2]]. For agents, Foundry separates system-level evaluators from process-level ones that point at a step [[r3]].

explain.title: Where each score attaches
explain.alt: A query passes through retrieval, generation and tool use to an answer. Rank metrics score retrieval, groundedness scores generation, tool accuracy scores tool use, and a correctness score judges the final answer.
explain.src:
flowchart LR
  Q[Query] --> R[Retrieve]
  R --> G[Generate]
  G --> T[Tools]
  T --> A[Answer]
  R -.-> M1[Rank metrics]
  G -.-> M2[Groundedness]
  T -.-> M3[Tool accuracy]
  A -.-> M4[End-to-end score]

explain.title: Freeze the upstream
explain.md: To test generation alone, feed it gold or recorded contexts. To test retrieval alone, score the ranked list and stop. Both isolate a fault without waiting for a full run.

whereToUse: RAG systems, where retrieval and generation fail for different reasons
Agents with several tools, where a single bad call can ruin the outcome
Pipelines with a router, reranker or guardrail that has its own error rate
CI, where cheap component checks gate every change and end-to-end runs nightly

use: More than one stage can cause the same bad answer
You change one stage at a time (new retriever, new prompt)
You need a fast check on every commit
avoid: Treating component scores as proof users are happy
Building a metric for every stage when one stage has never failed
Skipping an end-to-end check because every component score looks healthy
flips: Interaction effects dominate (context order, truncation): raise the share of end-to-end checks
Few labels exist: lean on end-to-end rubric judges and add component labels as failures appear
A stage is a managed black box you cannot isolate: test it end to end with fixed inputs

pitfalls.symptom: Every component score is green but the answers are poor
pitfalls.cause: Interaction between stages, such as context order or prompt truncation, which no isolated test exercises
pitfalls.fix: Keep an end-to-end set and compare its trend with component trends

pitfalls.symptom: The team chases ten dashboards and false alarms
pitfalls.cause: Too many component metrics, so some move by chance
pitfalls.fix: Choose one primary metric per layer and gate on those

pitfalls.symptom: A generation fix appears to fail
pitfalls.cause: Retrieval was also changing, so the test was not isolated
pitfalls.fix: Freeze retrieved contexts when testing generation

scenarios.title: Quality dropped after a retriever swap
scenarios.situation: A RAG assistant's end-to-end pass rate fell from 82% to 74% the day the team replaced its retriever. Nothing else shipped. Both versions are in a staging environment.
constraints: A labelled query set with relevant document ids exists
unknowns: Did recall at the sent k drop, or ranking?
Are the failures concentrated in some query types?
scenarios.question: What do you run first?

options.name: Retrieval metrics on the labelled queries for old and new retriever
options.why: Only retrieval changed, so a recall and ranking comparison at the real k localises the fault in minutes and at low cost.
options.tradeoff: It shows retrieval quality, not whether a different prompt could compensate.

options.name: Rerun the full end-to-end suite with more judges
options.why: It repeats the symptom and costs more without naming the layer.
options.tradeoff: More judges help when the question is whether the final answer is acceptable, not where it broke.

options.name: Tune the generation prompt to recover the score
options.why: A prompt can mask weaker context.
options.tradeoff: It hides a retrieval regression and may fail on queries the new retriever misses entirely.

flips.then: Look at generation with contexts frozen, then at context formatting and truncation.
Use judged context metrics while you label a small query set.

scenarios.takeaway: Change one stage, check that stage first.

scenarios.title: Tool-using agent in CI
scenarios.situation: An agent with six tools runs in CI on every pull request. A full multi-turn evaluation takes 40 minutes and costs real judge tokens. Engineers merge 30 times a day.
constraints: Tool calls have stable, checkable arguments
unknowns: Is there an outcome check available in a sandbox?
How flaky is the full run?
scenarios.question: How do you split checks between pull requests and nightly runs?

options.name: Code-based tool and argument checks on a small set per PR, full end-to-end nightly
options.why: Cheap deterministic checks give fast feedback on the most common breakage, and the expensive run stays off the critical path.
options.tradeoff: Some interaction failures appear a day late.

options.name: Full end-to-end on every PR
options.why: It blocks 30 merges a day for 40 minutes and burns budget.
options.tradeoff: Fine for a weekly release branch with few merges.

options.name: Only manual review of a few traces each week
options.tradeoff: No regression gate, and it does not scale with merges.

flips.if: Merges drop to a few a week
flips.then: Run the end-to-end suite on every PR.

flips.if: A tool can change real data
flips.then: Add an outcome check in an isolated environment before merge.

scenarios.takeaway: Run cheap component checks often and end-to-end checks on a slower cadence.

quiz.q: Recall@5 is high and groundedness is high, yet users report wrong answers. What is the most plausible gap?
options: The retrieved documents may be wrong or outdated, so a faithful answer can still be incorrect
quiz.explain: Groundedness checks consistency with the retrieved context, not truth. If the context is wrong or stale, the answer is faithful and wrong. High recall rules out option one, and the others are not implied.

quiz.q: You can afford one new check this sprint. Retrieval and generation both look fine in spot checks, but the agent sometimes calls the wrong tool. Which check?
options: Tool selection accuracy on labelled intents
quiz.explain: The suspected fault is tool selection, so a component check on it localises the problem cheaply. A bigger end-to-end suite repeats the symptom, and retrieval is not suspected.

quiz.q: Match each stage to a component-level check.

pairs.r: Attack success rate on a probe set

quiz.explain: Each component check holds the other stages fixed so a drop is attributable to that stage.

flashcards.front: Why keep both component and end-to-end evals?
flashcards.back: Component scores localise a fault. End-to-end scores say whether users are affected. Only the second catches interaction effects such as context order or truncation.

flashcards.front: How do you test generation in isolation?
flashcards.back: Freeze the retrieved context (gold or recorded) and score only the answer, for example with groundedness and completeness.

flashcards.front: What are Hamel Husain's three eval levels?
flashcards.back: Fast assertions on every change, model and human evaluation on a cadence, and A/B tests after significant product changes. Cost rises at each level.
